title: The Physiologically Difficult Airway: Why Intubation Can Precipitate Collapse
summary: Why four patients with easy anatomy can still collapse around intubation, through a small oxygen store, failing venous return, lost compensatory ventilation, or a right ventricle with no reserve. Study material, not a protocol.
shareDescription: Why patients with easy anatomy can still collapse during intubation, and how oxygen stores, venous return, acidosis and the right ventricle explain it.

principles.title: Part I. Four patients, one procedure
body: Four adults in the same resuscitation room need a tracheal tube. Like the patients in the earlier chapters, they are hypothetical, built for teaching, and each weighs about 80 kg. None of them has an anatomically hard airway. A laryngoscopist would see the cords easily in all four. Each of them can still die during the next ten minutes, and for a different reason.

Patient H has pneumonia in several lobes. She is breathing 34 times a minute and her saturation is 88 percent on a non-rebreather mask. Patient P has been vomiting blood; his heart rate is 120, his blood pressure 90/50, and he is pale and slow to answer. Patient M has diabetic ketoacidosis. Her pH is 7.15, her bicarbonate 5 mmol/L, her PaCO2 15 mm Hg, and she is taking deep, rapid breaths at about 36 a minute. Patient R has a large pulmonary embolus. His heart rate is 115, his blood pressure 92/60, his central venous pressure 18 mm Hg, and his saturation 90 percent on oxygen.

The tube itself is not the danger. The danger is what happens to each patient's physiology between the moment we induce anesthesia and the moment we have restored, through the ventilator, what the patient was doing alone. This chapter follows those four patients through that interval, using the venous return model from the [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow) and the gas-exchange physiology of the [Acute Respiratory Failure chapter](/cases/acute-respiratory-failure#principle-oxygen-in). Anatomy, devices, laryngoscopy, and the choice and dosing of drugs belong elsewhere.

principles.title: What makes an airway physiologically difficult
body: An airway is called anatomically difficult when it is hard to see the larynx, place a tube, or ventilate with a mask. An airway is physiologically difficult when the patient's own physiology makes collapse likely around intubation, however easy the mechanics. The term was set out for emergency medicine by Mosier and colleagues, and the Society for Airway Management later published consensus recommendations around it. The two kinds of difficulty are independent. A patient can have either, both, or neither, and planning for one does nothing for the other.

Collapse here has three faces: oxygen saturation falling to a dangerous level, blood pressure falling to a level that cannot sustain organ perfusion, and cardiac arrest. They are linked. Profound hypoxemia can stop the heart, and a failing circulation delivers less oxygen and empties the oxygen store faster. In the four patients, one face of collapse is likely to arrive first, and knowing which one is the point of the next six parts.

principles.title: What intubation takes away and what it adds
body: A useful way to picture intubation is as reducing or removing three things and adding two. This is a teaching frame rather than a fixed rule: how much each element matters depends on the patient, the drugs chosen and the doses given. The first thing removed is spontaneous breathing. While a patient breathes, every breath both brings in oxygen and carries out carbon dioxide, and the pattern of breathing is often doing compensatory work, as in Patient M. The second is sympathetic tone. A patient in shock is held up by high sympathetic activity that narrows arterioles, tightens veins and drives the heart. Most induction regimens lower that tone, to a degree that differs between agents, doses and patients, and relief of distress lowers it further. The third is negative intrathoracic pressure. Each spontaneous breath lowers the pressure around the heart and helps blood return to it.

The first thing added is apnea. Between induction and the first effective ventilation, oxygen is consumed from a fixed store and carbon dioxide accumulates. The second is positive pressure. Once ventilation starts through the tube, intrathoracic pressure rises with every breath instead of falling, which raises right atrial pressure, and lung inflation stretches the pulmonary vessels.

Spontaneous breathing is not free, however. A large negative swing in pleural pressure also raises the pressure the left ventricle must generate relative to its surroundings, adding to its afterload, and labored breathing consumes oxygen and cardiac output of its own. The [Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Edema chapter](/cases/cardiogenic-pulmonary-edema#principle-work-of-breathing) develops that side of the balance. In the four patients here, what intubation takes away usually matters more than what it relieves, which is why the next part starts with the losses.

Each of the four patients depends heavily on one of the things that is taken away or is badly hurt by one of the things that is added. Patient H has a reduced oxygen store (about 1.2 L in the worked example), uses it quickly, and needs her own breathing to keep refilling it. Patient P needs sympathetic tone and the help that negative pressure gives venous return. Patient M needs her very high ventilation, because it is holding her pH up. Patient R needs a low pulmonary vascular resistance and a systemic pressure high enough to perfuse his right ventricle, and apnea and positive pressure threaten both.

questions.prompt: A woman at 38 weeks of pregnancy with pre-eclampsia and no lung disease needs intubation. Which of the three things removed and two things added would you expect to matter most for her, and why?
questions.answer: Apnea matters most for oxygen. Late pregnancy shrinks her FRC, because the uterus pushes the diaphragm up, and raises her oxygen consumption, so her oxygen store is small and used quickly, much as in Patient H though for a different reason. Loss of spontaneous breathing also matters, because pregnancy normally lowers PaCO2, and an ordinary ventilator setting may let it rise. Positive pressure and loss of tone matter for pressure, particularly if she lies flat and the uterus compresses the great veins, which lowers venous return as in Patient P.
questions.causalChain: Pregnancy reduces FRC and raises consumption; the apnea clock is short; physiological hyperventilation is lost with apnea; supine caval compression plus positive pressure and lower tone reduce venous return.
questions.assumption: That she has no lung disease and that her blood pressure is not severely raised or falling at the time.
questions.misconception: That a patient with healthy lungs has a long safe apnea time.

diagram.caption: Figure 1. What intubation can reduce or add. Three things that can be reduced or removed (spontaneous breathing, sympathetic tone, which is often reduced, and negative intrathoracic pressure) and two added (apnea, positive pressure), each linked to the patient it threatens most: H, with a reduced oxygen store of about 1.2 L, P, M and R. A conceptual teaching frame, not a timeline or a fixed rule; the size of each effect depends on the patient and the drugs used.

principles.title: How often collapse happens
body: Peri-intubation collapse is common in critically ill adults. INTUBE, a prospective observational study of 2,964 intubations at 197 sites in 29 countries, recorded at least one major adverse event within 30 minutes in 45.2 percent. Cardiovascular instability was the commonest, in 42.6 percent, defined broadly as a systolic pressure below 65 mm Hg once, below 90 mm Hg for more than 30 minutes, new or increased vasopressor use, or a large fluid requirement. Severe hypoxemia, a saturation below 80 percent, occurred in 9.3 percent, and cardiac arrest in 3.1 percent.

Single-center data tell a similar story. In a retrospective study of 410 emergency department intubations, Heffner and colleagues found cardiac arrest in 4.2 percent, at a median of 6 minutes after intubation. Arrest was more common in patients who were hypotensive before intubation (12 vs 3 percent), and the pre-intubation shock index was independently associated with arrest. These are associations from observational data. They describe which patients are at risk, not what would prevent the event.

questions.prompt: Before any drug is given, predict which form of collapse is most likely to come first in each of the four patients.
questions.answer: Patient H is most likely to desaturate first, because consolidation has shrunk her oxygen store, her consumption is high, and blood flowing through her unventilated lung bypasses even well-filled alveoli, so she starts at the shoulder of the curve. Patient P is most likely to become hypotensive first, as sympathetic tone falls and positive pressure can reduce his venous return. Patient M is at risk of a fall in pH that can cause hemodynamic collapse and arrest, because apnea and an ordinary ventilator setting remove her respiratory compensation. Patient R is at risk of right ventricular failure spiraling into arrest, because hypoxemia and hypercapnia during apnea raise pulmonary vascular resistance while induction lowers the pressure that perfuses his right ventricle.
questions.causalChain: Each patient depends on something intubation removes or is harmed by something it adds: H on her own breathing to sustain a small store while shunt lowers her starting saturation; P on sympathetic tone and negative intrathoracic pressure; M on very high ventilation; R on low pulmonary vascular resistance and adequate systemic pressure.
questions.assumption: That none of the four has an anatomically difficult airway, so the timing is set by physiology rather than by a long attempt.
questions.misconception: That an easy view of the larynx means a safe intubation.

principles.title: Part II. Oxygen reserve and the clock during apnea
body: Once a patient stops breathing, the body runs on stored oxygen. How long that store lasts before the saturation starts to fall steeply is the safe apnea time. A first estimate rests on two quantities: how much oxygen is stored and how fast it is consumed. Both can be estimated, and both vary a great deal between patients. Shunt, the starting oxygenation and any oxygen that enters during apnea then decide how closely the saturation follows that estimate.

principles.title: Where oxygen is stored
body: The body holds oxygen in three places. The largest adjustable store is the gas in the lungs at the end of a normal breath out, the functional residual capacity (FRC). In a healthy adult lying flat it is roughly 2.5 liters. The second store is the blood, mostly bound to hemoglobin. The third, small for our purposes, is oxygen dissolved in tissue and bound to myoglobin.

The blood store cannot be enlarged much. Hemoglobin in arterial blood is already nearly saturated on room air, so breathing pure oxygen adds only the small dissolved fraction. The lung store is different. On room air, the alveolar gas is mostly nitrogen and holds only about 14 percent oxygen. Replace that nitrogen with oxygen and the same volume of gas holds about six times as much. That replacement is what preoxygenation does, and it is why FRC is the store that matters most for apnea.

Several common conditions shrink the FRC. Lying flat lets the abdominal contents push the diaphragm up. Obesity and late pregnancy do the same more strongly. Consolidation, edema and collapse take whole regions of lung out of the store, as in Patient H. At the same time, fever, sepsis, high work of breathing and agitation raise oxygen consumption. A small store and a fast rate of use together shorten the clock from both ends.

principles.title: The clock: store divided by consumption
body: Dividing the oxygen in the lungs by the rate of oxygen consumption gives a simple depletion estimate: how long the lung store alone would last if nothing were added and nothing changed. It is neither a prediction nor a true upper limit. Saturation does not wait for the store to empty: as alveolar oxygen falls, arterial oxygen tension falls with it, and once it reaches the steep part of the dissociation curve the saturation drops quickly while plenty of oxygen remains in the lungs. In the other direction, oxygen drawn in through an open airway during apnea can extend the interval beyond the estimate. Modeling studies by Farmery and Roe, and by Benumof and colleagues, describe how desaturation unfolds over time, and both show it beginning well before the lung store is used up, sooner in patients who are sick, obese or small.

The worked example shows the arithmetic for a healthy adult after good preoxygenation, for the same adult on room air, and for Patient H. The difference between the first two is the whole case for preoxygenation. The difference between the healthy adult and Patient H is the reason preoxygenation alone may not protect her.

questions.prompt: A healthy adult and Patient H begin apnea at the same moment, both after the best preoxygenation each can achieve. Predict whose saturation falls first and explain it in terms of store and consumption.
questions.answer: Patient H's saturation falls first, and probably much sooner. Her store is smaller because consolidated lung holds no gas and so is not part of the FRC. Her ventilated alveoli can be well denitrogenated, but a leaking mask and very high inspiratory flow may keep her short of a full fill. Her consumption is likely higher because of fever and work of breathing. Most important, shunted blood bypasses the store altogether, so she starts at 88 percent, on the steep part of the curve, where even a small fall in PaO2 produces a large fall in saturation. The healthy adult starts with a store of about 2.2 liters, at a saturation near 100 percent, on the flat part of the curve.
questions.causalChain: Smaller aerated volume gives a smaller store; mask leak may limit filling; higher consumption empties it faster; shunt lowers the starting saturation, so a small fall in PaO2 becomes a large fall in saturation.
questions.assumption: That both have similar hemoglobin and that neither receives any ventilation or apneic oxygen during the interval.
questions.misconception: That the time to desaturation is the same for everyone who has been preoxygenated.

diagram.caption: Figure 2. The apnea clock. Lung oxygen store against time for three cases: a healthy adult after preoxygenation (about 2.2 L, estimate about 8.7 minutes at 250 mL/min), the same adult on room air (about 0.35 L, estimate about 1.4 minutes), and Patient H, whose store is smaller and whose saturation is already near the steep part of the curve; no estimate is given for her. Each is a simple depletion estimate, store divided by consumption: not an upper limit and not a time to a saturation of 90 percent. Saturation falls before the store is empty. Schematic.
diagram.alt: Three downward-sloping lines showing lung oxygen store falling over time. The top line starts at about 2.2 liters and reaches zero near 8.7 minutes. The middle line starts at about 0.35 liters and reaches zero near 1.4 minutes. A third, dashed line for Patient H starts lower than the top line, falls faster and has no estimate; it is marked early with a shaded band showing where saturation begins to fall steeply. A note reads: depletion estimates, not upper limits and not times to a saturation of 90 percent.

workedExample.title: Worked example: three oxygen stores
body: These numbers are illustrative and assume an adult of about 80 kg at sea level, oxygen consumption 250 mL/min, and no ventilation and no oxygen inflow during apnea. Each is a simplified depletion estimate of the lung store, not an upper limit and not a time to a saturation of 90 percent.

**Healthy adult, preoxygenated.** FRC about 2.5 L. After good preoxygenation, alveolar oxygen fraction about 0.87 (below the theoretical maximum, which is deliberately conservative). Lung oxygen = 2.5 × 0.87 ≈ 2.2 L. Estimate = 2.2 / 0.25 ≈ 8.7 minutes.
**Same adult, room air.** Alveolar oxygen fraction about 0.14 (a PAO2 of about 100 mm Hg out of 713). Lung oxygen = 2.5 × 0.14 = 0.35 L. Estimate = 0.35 / 0.25 = 1.4 minutes.

**Patient H.** FRC reduced to about 1.5 L by consolidation, an illustrative value. Even if her ventilated alveoli reached an oxygen fraction of 0.8, the store would be about 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 L, and her consumption is likely to be higher than 250 mL/min. More important, her saturation is 88 percent before apnea begins, which at a normal pH means a PaO2 of roughly 55 to 60 mm Hg. She is already at the shoulder of the dissociation curve, so the saturation can fall steeply almost as soon as apnea starts. No single number of seconds can be given for her, because it depends on her shunt fraction, consumption and hemoglobin, none of which is known precisely.

**What the comparison shows.** Preoxygenation multiplies the estimate about sixfold in a healthy lung. In Patient H the store is smaller, may be incompletely filled if the mask leaks or cannot meet her inspiratory flow, and is drawn down from a starting point where the curve is already steep.

principles.title: Why the fall speeds up
body: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve is flat at the top and steep in the middle. Above a PaO2 of about 60 mm Hg, large falls in tension produce small falls in saturation, so a patient can lose much of the lung store while the monitor barely changes. Below that point, each further fall in PaO2 removes much more oxygen from hemoglobin. The saturation then drops quickly, and the oximeter, which averages over several seconds and sits on a finger downstream of the lungs, reports the fall late.

Acidemia and a rising PaCO2 shift the curve to the right, as described in the [Acute Respiratory Failure chapter](/cases/acute-respiratory-failure#principle-pulse-oximetry). During apnea PaCO2 rises steadily, so the curve moves rightward while PaO2 falls, and saturation drops further for any given tension. In Patient M, who starts severely acidemic, and in Patient R, who has little reserve, this matters more.

questions.prompt: During an intubation attempt, the saturation reads 93 percent and has been stable for a minute. Thirty seconds later it reads 78 percent. Explain why the fall seemed sudden.
questions.answer: The fall was not sudden in the lungs. Alveolar and arterial oxygen tension had been falling steadily throughout apnea, but while PaO2 stayed above about 60 mm Hg the flat upper part of the curve kept saturation high. Once PaO2 crossed onto the steep part, each further fall removed a large amount of oxygen from hemoglobin. The oximeter's averaging delay and its position downstream of the lungs make the visible drop appear later and steeper still. Rising PaCO2 during apnea shifts the curve rightward and adds to the effect.
questions.causalChain: Steady fall in PaO2; flat curve hides the early fall; steep curve below about 60 mm Hg; rightward shift from rising PaCO2; oximeter lag; apparent sudden drop.
questions.assumption: That the probe has a good signal and that no other event, such as a new pneumothorax, occurred in those 30 seconds.
questions.misconception: That a stable saturation means the oxygen store is stable.

principles.title: What shunt does to preoxygenation
body: Three different quantities are easy to run together here. The first is the volume of aerated lung, which sets the size of the store. The second is the oxygen fraction in the gas within those aerated alveoli, which preoxygenation raises by washing out nitrogen. The third is the fraction of pulmonary blood flow that actually passes ventilated alveoli. Shunt is about the third. Blood flowing through consolidated, unventilated lung never meets alveolar gas. It reaches the left heart with the oxygen content of mixed venous blood and lowers the content of the well-oxygenated blood from healthy lung. Shunt does not stop ventilated alveoli from filling with oxygen: in Patient H those alveoli can be nearly free of nitrogen while her arterial saturation stays low. As the [Acute Respiratory Failure chapter](/cases/acute-respiratory-failure#principle-vq-shunt) explains, the response of shunt to added oxygen is graded and limited, and it shrinks as the shunt fraction grows.

For Patient H this has three consequences. First, a high oxygen fraction in her exhaled gas shows that her ventilated lung is denitrogenated, but it says nothing about how much of her blood passes that lung, so a good end-tidal reading can sit beside a poor PaO2. Second, her saturation rises only modestly with preoxygenation, so she does not gain the margin a healthy patient gains. Third, her arterial saturation depends partly on her mixed venous oxygen content. When apnea starts and her consumption continues, mixed venous content falls, the shunted blood is more desaturated, and her arterial saturation falls faster than the lung store alone would predict. Raising the inspired oxygen further helps little. Ventilating more of her lung helps more, to the extent that her lung can be recruited, which is the reason positive pressure appears in the next part.

principles.title: Part III. Filling the store
body: Preoxygenation has one job: to replace nitrogen in the lungs with oxygen so that the store at the start of apnea is as large as it can be. How well that works depends on the inspired oxygen fraction actually reaching the alveoli, the time allowed, and whether the lung being filled is open.

principles.title: Denitrogenation and what limits it
body: Nitrogen leaves the lungs only as fast as it is breathed out. With each breath of pure oxygen, a fraction of the remaining nitrogen is replaced, so the alveolar oxygen fraction rises quickly at first and then levels off. Any entrained room air keeps bringing nitrogen back. A face mask that does not seal, or a non-rebreather whose flow cannot meet a patient's very high inspiratory flow, delivers far less oxygen than the setting implies. A distressed patient like Patient H, breathing at 34 a minute with large breaths, can easily draw room air around a loose mask.

The oxygen fraction in exhaled gas at the end of a breath shows how far denitrogenation has gone. Weingart and Levitan describe its use in emergency preoxygenation, and UK critical-care intubation guidelines use an end-tidal oxygen above 85 percent as the marker of adequate preoxygenation, and many clinicians aim for about 90 percent. The reading shows that the ventilated lung is denitrogenated. It does not show that arterial blood is well oxygenated, because shunted blood never meets that gas.

principles.title: Positive pressure before apnea
body: When shunt and a small aerated volume limit preoxygenation, the aim is to open more lung before apnea begins. Positive pressure through a tight-fitting mask, as non-invasive ventilation, can help in three ways. The seal stops room air entering, so the inspired fraction is close to that set. Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) can recruit some collapsed alveoli, enlarging the aerated volume and, where recruitment succeeds, returning some shunted blood flow to ventilated lung. It does not open every alveolus: consolidated or fluid-filled units may not open at all, and how much a given lung recruits cannot be known in advance. And pressure support on each breath reduces the work of breathing, which lowers oxygen consumption. In a small study of 40 healthy elective surgical patients, 6 cm H2O of positive pressure during preoxygenation and induction lengthened apnea to a saturation of 90 percent by about 2 minutes, plausibly by preserving aerated lung volume. That is evidence about the size of the store, not about shunt.

PREOXI tested this in critically ill adults undergoing tracheal intubation at 24 sites in the United States. Of 1,301 patients randomized, 645 were assigned to non-invasive ventilation and 656 to an oxygen mask. The primary outcome, hypoxemia defined as a saturation below 85 percent between induction and 2 minutes after intubation, occurred in 57 of 624 (9.1 percent) and 118 of 637 (18.5 percent) patients with outcome data. Cardiac arrest occurred in 1 of 645 (0.2 percent) and 7 of 656 (1.1 percent), and aspiration in 6 of 645 (0.9 percent) and 9 of 656 (1.4 percent), a difference that was not statistically significant.

In PREOXI, then, non-invasive ventilation roughly halved hypoxemia below 85 percent in critically ill adults who were not already on positive pressure and were not vomiting or bleeding into the airway. That supports it over an oxygen mask for patients like those enrolled. Aspiration was uncommon in both groups and not significantly different, but the confidence interval does not establish equal safety, and patients judged at high aspiration risk were largely excluded.

questions.prompt: Patient H is changed from a non-rebreather mask to non-invasive ventilation with positive end-expiratory pressure for several minutes before induction. Predict what happens to her saturation and to her safe apnea time, and explain why.
questions.answer: Her saturation is likely to rise somewhat, and her safe apnea time is likely to lengthen. The tight seal raises the inspired fraction close to that set. PEEP may recruit some collapsed alveoli; where it does, her aerated volume grows, part of her shunted flow returns to ventilated lung, and arterial oxygen rises. Pressure support lowers her work of breathing and so her oxygen consumption. A larger store drawn down more slowly, starting from a higher point on the curve, gives a longer interval before saturation falls steeply. How large the effect is depends on how much of her consolidated lung can be recruited, and for lung filled with pus it may be small.
questions.causalChain: Seal raises inspired fraction; PEEP recruits whatever lung is recruitable, enlarging the store and reducing shunt in proportion; less work lowers consumption; a higher starting saturation moves her off the steep part of the curve.
questions.assumption: That some of her consolidated lung is recruitable and that she tolerates the mask.
questions.misconception: That a non-rebreather mask delivers nearly pure oxygen to a patient with high inspiratory flow.

questions.prompt: A colleague says PREOXI proves non-invasive ventilation is safe for preoxygenation in all critically ill patients, including those at high risk of aspiration. What does the trial show, and what does it not show?
questions.answer: PREOXI shows that in critically ill adults undergoing intubation at 24 US sites, non-invasive ventilation reduced hypoxemia below 85 percent from 18.5 percent to 9.1 percent compared with an oxygen mask. It does not establish equal safety for aspiration. Aspiration occurred in 0.9 percent with non-invasive ventilation and 1.4 percent with a mask, a difference that was not statistically significant, and the confidence interval is too wide to show the risks are the same. Patients already receiving positive pressure, those whose intubation was too urgent to randomize, and those with vomiting, hematemesis, hemoptysis or epistaxis were largely excluded, so the result does not extend to the patients the colleague is asking about.
questions.causalChain: Primary outcome is hypoxemia, not aspiration; a non-significant difference in a secondary safety outcome is not proof of no difference; generalization depends on who was enrolled.
questions.assumption: That the patient in question resembles those the trial enrolled.
questions.misconception: That absence of a statistically significant difference means proven equivalence.

principles.title: Oxygen during apnea
body: Oxygen continues to leave the alveoli during apnea, at about 250 mL/min in a resting adult, but carbon dioxide enters them much more slowly, because most of it stays dissolved and buffered in blood and tissue. That mismatch lowers alveolar pressure slightly and draws gas inward through an open airway. If the gas at the top of the airway is oxygen, delivered by nasal cannula, the store can be partly topped up without any breaths. This is apneic oxygenation. Patel and Nouraei described a high-flow nasal technique, THRIVE, in patients with difficult airways undergoing surgery.

In critically ill patients, the evidence is less encouraging. FELLOW randomized 150 adults in one medical intensive care unit to 15 L/min of 100 percent oxygen through a nasal cannula during laryngoscopy, or to usual care. The lowest saturation was a median of 92 percent with apneic oxygenation and 90 percent without it, a difference that was not statistically significant. The authors note that conduct in one medical ICU at a single academic center may limit generalizability, and that high compliance with preoxygenation, including non-invasive ventilation for patients with hypoxemia, may have reduced the potential benefit. The trial tested one technique, a 15 L/min cannula after good preoxygenation at one center, not every heated, humidified high-flow strategy. For a patient like Patient H, apneic oxygenation can add oxygen only to the ventilated alveoli; it does nothing for the blood that bypasses them.

Apneic oxygenation does nothing for carbon dioxide. Without breaths, carbon dioxide is not removed, and PaCO2 rises throughout apnea, at a rate that varies with metabolism and with how much carbon dioxide the blood and tissues can absorb. Even a modest rise matters for Patient M and Patient R.

questions.prompt: A patient with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and a PaCO2 of 70 mm Hg is preoxygenated and given nasal oxygen during a prolonged intubation attempt. His saturation stays at 95 percent throughout. Why might he still be in danger?
questions.answer: Apneic oxygenation can keep his saturation up while doing nothing to remove carbon dioxide. Throughout the attempt PaCO2 keeps rising from an already high starting point, so his pH falls further. Severe acidemia can depress myocardial function, cause arrhythmia, raise pulmonary vascular resistance and strain his right ventricle, and lower his conscious level after the procedure. The monitor shows oxygen only, so a reassuring saturation hides a worsening problem.
questions.causalChain: Oxygen uptake continues by mass flow; carbon dioxide is not removed without ventilation; PaCO2 rises; pH falls; acidemia harms the heart and pulmonary circulation; saturation does not show it.
questions.assumption: That he receives no effective ventilation during the attempt.
questions.misconception: That a normal saturation means gas exchange is adequate.

principles.title: Breaths between induction and laryngoscopy
body: Traditionally, patients were not ventilated with a bag and mask between induction and laryngoscopy, for fear of inflating the stomach and causing aspiration. Ventilating during that interval does three things: it adds oxygen to the store, removes some carbon dioxide, and may hold some recruited alveoli open.

PreVent randomized 401 critically ill adults in 7 intensive care units to bag-mask ventilation or no ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy. The lowest saturation was a median of 96 percent with ventilation and 93 percent without it. Severe hypoxemia, a secondary outcome defined as a saturation below 80 percent, occurred in 10.9 percent with ventilation and 22.8 percent without. Aspiration was 2.5 percent and 4.0 percent, and a new opacity on chest radiograph was 16.4 percent and 14.8 percent, neither difference statistically significant. The trial supports ventilation in that interval for patients like those enrolled. It does not show that aspiration risk is unchanged: by the authors' own estimate, about 4,000 patients would be needed to test that, and the trial had 401. Most enrolled patients had at least one risk factor for aspiration, but patients whose clinicians judged ventilation contraindicated because of ongoing vomiting, hematemesis or hemoptysis were excluded, so the result does not extend to them. Patient P, who is vomiting blood, may be exactly that kind of patient.

principles.title: Part IV. Why pressure falls after induction
body: Hypotension after intubation is the commonest form of peri-intubation collapse. It is not one mechanism but the sum of several, all acting within the first minutes: loss of sympathetic tone, the direct effects of induction drugs on vessels and heart, and the change from negative to positive intrathoracic pressure. Patient P shows all three most clearly. The venous return model from the [Shock chapter](https://www.resusfirstprinciples.io/cases/shock-pressure-flow#principle-venous-return) is the way to see how they combine.

diagram.caption: Figure 3. One circulation, several pressure gradients (reused from the Shock chapter, Figure 1). Venous return depends on the gap between mean systemic filling pressure, a model quantity that cannot be measured directly at the bedside, and right atrial pressure. Induction lowers the upstream pressure by relaxing veins; positive pressure raises right atrial pressure and narrows that gap.
diagram.alt: Schematic loop with two hearts drawn as separate pumps. Arrows run in one direction: left ventricle to aorta and systemic arteries, through a narrowed resistance segment and a capillary bed, into wide veins, to the right atrium, right ventricle, pulmonary arteries, lung capillaries, pulmonary veins, left atrium, and back to the left ventricle. Labels mark the systemic gradient from aorta to right atrium and the pulmonary gradient from pulmonary artery to left atrium.

principles.title: Sympathetic tone and what induction removes
body: A patient in shock maintains blood pressure through a strong sympathetic response. Arterioles constrict, raising resistance. Veins constrict, which moves blood from the stressed and unstressed venous reservoirs toward the heart and raises mean systemic filling pressure. Heart rate and contractility rise. In Patient P, who has lost blood, that response is holding his pressure at 90/50 despite a much reduced circulating volume.

Most induction agents reduce sympathetic outflow, and many also relax vascular smooth muscle or depress the myocardium directly, but the size of each effect differs between agents, doses and patients. Analgesic and sedative agents add to it in varying degree. Relief of pain, distress and the work of breathing removes part of the stimulus that was driving the sympathetic response. Any one of these can lower resistance, venous tone, or cardiac output. A patient whose pressure depends on high tone loses more of it than a patient who started calm.

principles.title: Venous return and positive pressure
body: As the Shock chapter explains, venous return is driven by the difference between mean systemic filling pressure and right atrial pressure. Mean systemic filling pressure is a model quantity: the pressure the circulation would settle at if flow stopped, set by the stressed blood volume and the stiffness of the vessels. It cannot be read from a bedside monitor, but it explains the direction of change. Right atrial pressure is the pressure against which blood returns. Cardiac output cannot exceed venous return for long. Anything that lowers the upstream pressure or raises the downstream pressure reduces the flow back to the heart.

Intubation does both. Venodilation from induction and any loss of sympathetic tone move blood into the unstressed venous volume, lowering mean systemic filling pressure. Then positive pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure on every breath, which raises right atrial pressure. With a full circulation, the gradient narrows but stays large enough. With a depleted one, as in Patient P, the upstream pressure is low to begin with, and a small rise in right atrial pressure can remove a large share of the remaining gradient. Large tidal volumes, fast rates, high PEEP and gas trapping all raise mean intrathoracic pressure and so worsen this effect.

Spontaneous breathing worked the other way. Each breath lowered intrathoracic pressure and widened the gradient slightly. Paralysis and positive pressure remove that help at the same moment as induction lowers the upstream pressure.

questions.prompt: After Patient P is intubated, he is bagged rapidly with large breaths at about 30 a minute. Predict what happens to his blood pressure, using venous return.
questions.answer: His blood pressure is likely to fall, possibly steeply. Rapid, large breaths raise mean intrathoracic pressure and may not allow full exhalation, so right atrial pressure rises. His mean systemic filling pressure is already low from blood loss and has been lowered further by induction. With a low upstream pressure, a rise in the downstream pressure removes a large share of the gradient, venous return falls, and cardiac output and blood pressure fall with it. Slower, smaller breaths would reduce the effect.
questions.causalChain: Large rapid breaths raise mean intrathoracic pressure; right atrial pressure rises; mean systemic filling pressure is low; venous return gradient narrows; venous return and cardiac output fall; pressure falls.
questions.assumption: That his lungs are not obstructed and that no other cause, such as tension pneumothorax, appears.
questions.misconception: That more ventilation is always better for a patient who has just been intubated.

principles.title: The shock index as a warning
body: The shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure. A higher value suggests that the circulation is relying more on compensation. In observational studies of emergency intubation, including Heffner's, a higher pre-intubation shock index was associated with post-intubation arrest. It is a crude measure: it is affected by medications, pain and the patient's usual pressure, and it cannot say which mechanism is failing.

Patient P has a heart rate of 120 and a systolic pressure of 90, a shock index of 1.33, and a mean arterial pressure of about 63 mm Hg. Patient R has a heart rate of 115 and a systolic pressure of 92, a shock index of 1.25, and a mean pressure of about 71 mm Hg. Both values are high, but for different reasons. Patient P's circulation is underfilled. Patient R's is held back by a right ventricle that cannot push blood through his lungs, and his central venous pressure of 18 mm Hg shows the downstream pressure is already high. The same number points to different dangers.

questions.prompt: A man with sepsis from a urinary source has a heart rate of 110 and a blood pressure of 140/80 before intubation. He takes a beta-blocker at home. What does his shock index tell you, and what might it miss?
questions.answer: His shock index is about 0.79, which looks reassuring. It might miss a great deal. His beta-blocker limits how high his heart rate can rise, so the numerator understates his sympathetic response. If his usual blood pressure is much higher, as in long-standing hypertension, a systolic of 140 may already be low for him. Sepsis lowers vascular tone, and induction and positive pressure may remove the compensation that remains. The index is a screening sign, not a measure of reserve.
questions.causalChain: Shock index = heart rate / systolic pressure; a drug that limits heart rate lowers the index without improving reserve; a high usual pressure makes a normal reading relatively low; sepsis reduces tone.
questions.assumption: That his blood pressure reading is accurate and that he has taken his usual beta-blocker dose.
questions.misconception: That a normal shock index rules out post-intubation hypotension.

principles.title: Fluid before induction
body: If low mean systemic filling pressure is part of the problem, it seems natural to give fluid before induction to raise it. PREPARE II tested this. In 11 intensive care units, 1,067 critically ill adults receiving positive-pressure ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy were randomized, and 1,065 were analyzed, to a 500 mL crystalloid bolus or no fluid bolus. Cardiovascular collapse occurred in 21.0 percent with the bolus and 18.2 percent without it, a difference that was not statistically significant.

In patients receiving positive-pressure ventilation during intubation, then, a routine 500 mL bolus did not significantly decrease cardiovascular collapse. About one in ten (109 of 1,065, 10.2 percent) had gastrointestinal bleeding as a baseline condition at enrollment, but patients whose clinician judged that a fluid bolus was required, or should be avoided, were excluded, as were intubations too urgent for the trial procedures. The authors add that the trial does not inform the use of fluid in critical illness outside the period immediately surrounding tracheal intubation. So it does not show that fluid is useless for a patient who is actually hypovolemic. For Patient P, the useful question is the one from the Shock chapter: is his circulation underfilled, and will added volume raise his output? Blood loss makes the answer more likely to be yes, and blood is the volume he has lost.

questions.prompt: A colleague cites PREPARE II and says Patient P should receive no fluid before induction. What does the trial show, and does it apply to him?
questions.answer: PREPARE II randomized 1,067 critically ill adults in 11 ICUs, all receiving positive-pressure ventilation during intubation, to a 500 mL fluid bolus or none, and found cardiovascular collapse in 21.0 percent and 18.2 percent, not a significant difference. A routine bolus did not significantly decrease collapse in the patients it enrolled, about one in ten of whom (109 of 1,065) had gastrointestinal bleeding as a baseline condition at enrollment. It excluded patients whose clinician judged that fluid was required. It does not show that fluid is useless in a patient whose circulation is clearly underfilled. Patient P is bleeding, so his mean systemic filling pressure is low because volume is missing. Restoring volume, ideally with blood, addresses that cause. The trial result does not answer his question, which is whether he is volume-responsive and what volume he has lost.
questions.causalChain: Patients judged to need fluid were excluded; benefit of fluid depends on volume responsiveness; a hemorrhaging patient is more likely to be underfilled; the evidence does not extend to him directly.
questions.assumption: That Patient P's clinicians would judge fluid to be required, which would have excluded him from the trial.
questions.misconception: That a neutral trial in a general population answers the question for every patient within it.

principles.title: Part V. When breathing is the treatment
body: Patient M is not short of oxygen. Her lungs are normal. Her danger is that her breathing is doing essential work that intubation will interrupt. Her pH of 7.15 is not a sign that her compensation has failed. It is the result of her compensation succeeding: without her very high ventilation, her pH would be far lower.

principles.title: Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis
body: In ketoacidosis, the accumulation of acids consumes bicarbonate. The body defends pH by lowering PaCO2, because pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide. Chemoreceptors sense the acidemia and drive ventilation up, often with the deep, rapid pattern described by Kussmaul. Lower PaCO2 partly restores the ratio.

The expected degree of compensation was described by Albert, Dell and Winters in 1967 and is known as Winter's formula: expected PaCO2 is about 1.5 × bicarbonate + 8, plus or minus 2. For Patient M, with a bicarbonate of 5 mmol/L, that gives 15.5 mm Hg, with a range of 13.5 to 17.5. Her measured PaCO2 of 15 lies within it, so her compensation is as complete as can be expected. Using the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, her pH is 6.1 + log(5 / (0.03 × 15)), which is about 7.15, matching the measured value.

questions.prompt: Patient M's bicarbonate stays at 5 mmol/L but her PaCO2 is measured at 25 mm Hg rather than 15. Predict her pH, and say what the higher PaCO2 would mean.
questions.answer: Her pH would be about 6.92, because 6.1 + log(5 / (0.03 × 25)) is 6.1 + log(6.67), about 6.92. Winter's formula predicts a PaCO2 of 13.5 to 17.5 for her bicarbonate, so a PaCO2 of 25 means her ventilation is falling short of what her acidosis demands. That points to an additional problem, such as fatigue, reduced drive from sedation or cerebral edema, or a lung or chest wall problem. Either way it is a sign of reduced reserve, not of improvement.
questions.causalChain: pH depends on the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved CO2; with fixed bicarbonate, a higher PaCO2 lowers pH; Winter's formula sets the expected PaCO2; a value above the range means inadequate compensation.
questions.assumption: That her bicarbonate is unchanged and that the measurement is from an arterial sample.
questions.misconception: That a higher PaCO2 is reassuring because it is closer to normal.

principles.title: What apnea and an ordinary ventilator do to her
body: During apnea, carbon dioxide is no longer removed and her PaCO2 starts to rise from 15 mm Hg. Two things make that rise dangerous for her. Her pH is already 7.15, so she has little room before acidemia becomes more severe still. And because her bicarbonate and her PaCO2 are both so low, each mm Hg of PaCO2 is a large proportional change in their ratio: holding her bicarbonate at 5 mmol/L to isolate the effect, a rise from 15 to 20 mm Hg alone lowers her pH by about 0.12, from 7.15 to about 7.02. Every second of apnea moves her pH downward from an already dangerous level.

After intubation, the ventilator sets her alveolar ventilation. An ordinary initial setting, designed for a patient with a normal PaCO2, delivers far less ventilation than she was producing on her own. The worked example shows the consequence. Severe acidemia depresses myocardial contractility, reduces vascular responsiveness to catecholamines, and predisposes to arrhythmia, as reviewed by Kimmoun and colleagues for acidosis in shock. There is no single pH below which collapse becomes inevitable. The risk rises as pH falls, and Patient M starts low.

workedExample.title: Worked example: Patient M on an ordinary ventilator setting
body: These numbers are illustrative. They assume a carbon dioxide production of about 200 mL/min, an anatomical dead space of 150 mL, and a fixed bicarbonate. Holding bicarbonate at 5 mmol/L isolates the effect of rising PaCO2 on the Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship. These values illustrate the danger of losing respiratory compensation; they do not predict the patient's pH or the time taken to reach it. Actual changes depend on buffering, CO2 stores, metabolism and treatment.
**What she needs.** To hold PaCO2 at 15 mm Hg she needs an alveolar ventilation of about 11.5 L/min. With a dead-space fraction of 0.3, that is a minute ventilation of about 16 L/min.

**What an ordinary setting gives.** A tidal volume of 450 mL at 16 breaths a minute gives 7.2 L/min of minute ventilation. Subtracting 150 mL of dead space from each breath leaves 300 mL × 16 = 4.8 L/min of alveolar ventilation, less than half of what she needs.

**A simplified steady-state estimate.** If that alveolar ventilation continued unchanged, PaCO2 = 0.863 × 200 / 4.8 ≈ 36 mm Hg, and with bicarbonate still at 5 mmol/L the pH would be 6.1 + log(5 / (0.03 × 36)), about 6.77. This assumes CO2 production of 200 mL/min, fixed dead space and fixed bicarbonate; it is not the PaCO2 or pH she will have in the first minutes after intubation, which depend on CO2 stores and buffering.

**The transition right after intubation.** Her PaCO2 climbs toward that estimate over minutes, along a path set by her CO2 stores and buffering, so only an early blood gas shows where she actually is. Under the same fixed-bicarbonate assumption, a PaCO2 of 25 mm Hg corresponds to a pH of about 6.92, and 40 mm Hg, which she would reach only if her ventilation were lower still, to about 6.72. A PaCO2 that would be normal in a healthy patient is, for her, one of the most dangerous values on the page.

**What the comparison shows.** The ventilator setting that suits most patients would remove most of her compensation. The quantity to restore is her alveolar ventilation, not a copy of her minute ventilation: the same minute ventilation delivered as smaller, faster breaths, or through added apparatus dead space, leaves less alveolar ventilation and a higher PaCO2.

principles.title: Matching her ventilation
body: The principle for Patient M is to keep the interval without ventilation as short as possible and then to give her enough alveolar ventilation to hold her PaCO2 near the low level she had reached herself, checked by a blood gas soon after. Her pre-intubation minute ventilation is a starting reference, not a target to copy, because dead space changes the PaCO2 produced by the same minute ventilation. Achieving it requires both a higher rate and an adequate tidal volume, and it is limited by the risk of gas trapping at very high rates, so the result must be measured, not assumed. Winter's formula told us how well she was compensating; it describes her, it does not prescribe a ventilator setting. Her end-tidal carbon dioxide can help trend the change between gases but does not replace an arterial or venous measurement.

This principle applies whenever spontaneous ventilation is compensating for a metabolic acidosis, whatever its cause. It also explains why some clinicians try to avoid intubating these patients when their consciousness and airway allow it, a judgment that rests with the treating team.

questions.prompt: A woman with salicylate poisoning has a pH of 7.38, a PaCO2 of 22 mm Hg, and is breathing very fast. She becomes drowsy and needs intubation. What does Patient M's case predict for her, and what extra concern does salicylate add?
questions.answer: Like Patient M, her very high ventilation is holding her pH up, and an ordinary ventilator setting would let her PaCO2 rise and her pH fall. With salicylate, a fall in pH has an extra consequence. More of the drug is in its non-ionized form at lower pH, so more crosses into the brain and other tissues, worsening toxicity. Keeping the interval without ventilation short and matching her pre-intubation ventilation, checked by early gases, is therefore even more important.
questions.causalChain: High spontaneous ventilation compensates for metabolic acidosis; loss of ventilation raises PaCO2 and lowers pH; lower pH increases the non-ionized salicylate fraction; more drug enters tissue; toxicity worsens.
questions.assumption: That her acidosis is predominantly metabolic and that the high ventilation is partly compensatory rather than solely a direct drug effect.
questions.misconception: That a near-normal pH means there is little to lose during intubation.

principles.title: Part VI. The right ventricle under load
body: Patient R's danger is the most self-reinforcing of the four. His right ventricle is already struggling against a pulmonary circulation obstructed by clot. Several things that happen during intubation make that load heavier at the moment the ventricle's own blood supply is reduced. The European statement on acute right ventricular failure by Harjola and colleagues describes how hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis raise right ventricular afterload, and why positive pressure and the sedation needed for intubation are hazardous. The perfusion-pressure approximation used below is a teaching simplification.

principles.title: A ventricle built for low pressure
body: The right ventricle is thin-walled and normally does low-pressure work, pumping the whole cardiac output into a circulation of low pressure and resistance. It tolerates increases in volume far better than increases in pressure. When pulmonary vascular resistance rises suddenly, as with a large embolus, the ventricle dilates, its wall stress and oxygen demand rise, and its stroke volume falls. Less blood reaches the left heart, so left ventricular filling and systemic output fall.

A dilated right ventricle also pushes the septum toward the left, which reduces left ventricular filling further. That interdependence is why Patient R's high central venous pressure of 18 mm Hg sits alongside a low systemic pressure: the right side is congested, while the left side is underfilled. Giving more volume can make this worse by dilating the right ventricle further.

principles.title: What intubation does to the pulmonary circulation
body: Hypoxemia constricts pulmonary arterioles. So do hypercapnia and acidemia. During apnea, both oxygen and carbon dioxide move in the wrong direction, so pulmonary vascular resistance rises at a time when Patient R has no reserve. Positive pressure adds a mechanical effect, and lung volume acts on resistance in two opposite directions. Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest near the normal resting lung volume. Collapsed lung raises it, through narrowing of the larger vessels outside the alveoli and through hypoxic vasoconstriction, so pressure that reopens collapsed lung can lower resistance. Overinflation raises it, by stretching and compressing the capillaries in the alveolar walls, so large tidal volumes or PEEP beyond what the lung needs add load. Positive pressure also raises right atrial pressure and so reduces venous return to a ventricle that is already working at the limit of its function.

At the same time, the drug classes used for induction reduce systemic vascular tone and may depress contractility. Each of these effects is modest on its own. Together, and in a patient with no reserve, they can be enough to tip the balance.

principles.title: Perfusion pressure and the spiral
body: The right ventricle receives its blood supply mainly from the right coronary artery. Its perfusion depends on the difference between aortic pressure and the pressure within the ventricular wall. Normally that wall pressure is low enough for the right ventricle to be perfused during both systole and diastole. When the ventricle is pressure-loaded and dilated, its wall pressure rises, systolic perfusion is lost, and the driving pressure narrows just as demand rises. A rough bedside illustration, used here for teaching, is mean arterial pressure minus central venous pressure. It shows the direction of change; it is not a measurement of right coronary flow, which varies through the cardiac cycle and with wall tension.

For Patient R, mean arterial pressure is about 71 mm Hg and central venous pressure 18 mm Hg, a difference of about 53 mm Hg. If induction lowers his mean pressure to 55 mm Hg with no change in central venous pressure, the difference falls to about 37 mm Hg. These numbers are illustrative. A ventricle that is working harder now receives less blood. Its contractility falls, its output falls, systemic pressure falls further, and perfusion falls again. This is the spiral that can turn a stable but strained patient into a cardiac arrest within minutes. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, lung collapse and overinflation push the same loop from the other side by raising pulmonary vascular resistance.

questions.prompt: Immediately after induction, Patient R's mean arterial pressure falls from 71 to 55 mm Hg and his saturation falls during a prolonged attempt. Predict what happens to his right ventricle and why it may not recover on its own.
questions.answer: His right ventricular perfusion, roughly illustrated by MAP minus CVP, falls from about 53 to about 37 mm Hg, so the ventricle receives less blood just as its workload rises. Falling saturation and rising PaCO2 during apnea raise pulmonary vascular resistance and add to that workload. The ventricle weakens, its output falls, left ventricular filling falls, and systemic pressure falls further, which lowers its perfusion again. Unless it is interrupted, by raising systemic pressure or lowering pulmonary vascular resistance, the loop can sustain itself.
questions.causalChain: Lower MAP reduces RV perfusion; hypoxemia and hypercapnia raise PVR; RV demand rises while supply falls; RV output falls; LV filling and systemic pressure fall; perfusion falls again.
questions.assumption: That his central venous pressure stays near 18 mm Hg and that the clot burden does not change.
questions.misconception: That a fall in pressure after induction in this patient is a transient drug effect that will correct itself.

questions.prompt: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension from chronic lung disease needs intubation. Using Patient R's case, which ventilator choices after intubation would you expect to worsen her right ventricular function?
questions.answer: Large tidal volumes, high plateau pressures and PEEP beyond what keeps her lung open would overinflate the lung, stretch the alveolar vessels and raise pulmonary vascular resistance, adding load to her right ventricle. High mean intrathoracic pressure would also raise right atrial pressure and reduce venous return. Too little PEEP can harm too, if lung collapses, because collapse and the hypoxic vasoconstriction that follows also raise resistance. Too little ventilation would allow hypercapnia and acidemia, which constrict the pulmonary vessels. Too little oxygen would add hypoxic vasoconstriction. The aim is to avoid all of these together, which usually means modest pressures with enough ventilation and oxygen, checked by measurement.
questions.causalChain: Overinflation and collapse both raise PVR; high intrathoracic pressure lowers venous return; hypercapnia, acidemia and hypoxemia constrict pulmonary vessels; RV afterload rises; RV failure follows.
questions.assumption: That her pulmonary hypertension is fixed in part but still responsive to these changes.
questions.misconception: That the same ventilator settings suit every patient after intubation.

diagram.caption: Figure 4. The right ventricular spiral. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, lung collapse and overinflation raise pulmonary vascular resistance and add right ventricular load. The loaded ventricle dilates and its wall stress rises; its perfusion and contraction fall; left ventricular filling and systemic pressure fall; and right ventricular perfusion falls further. Unless interrupted, the loop can sustain itself. Simplified teaching model.
diagram.alt: A directional loop: greater right ventricular load leads to dilation and wall stress, reduced right ventricular perfusion and contraction, reduced left ventricular filling and lower systemic pressure, which further reduces right ventricular perfusion. Hypoxemia, hypercapnia, lung collapse and overinflation feed in by raising pulmonary vascular resistance. Simplified teaching model; no values shown.

principles.title: Does Patient R need a tube?
body: Because each step of intubation threatens his right ventricle, the first question for Patient R is whether he needs a tube at all. If he is awake, protecting his airway, and his saturation can be held with oxygen or high-flow support, the danger of intubation may be greater than the danger of continued spontaneous breathing while the embolus is treated. If he is tiring, unable to protect his airway, or developing worsening hypoxemia despite support, the balance shifts. That judgment depends on the treatment available for the clot, on how quickly it can be given, and on local expertise, and it rests with the treating team. What the physiology adds is a clear account of what intubation would cost him.

principles.title: Part VII. After the tube
body: Placing the tube does not end the danger. In one series, Heffner and colleagues found a median time to arrest of about 6 minutes after intubation. The minutes after placement are when positive pressure is newly established and when attention tends to move to the next task.

The first minute after placement has its own checks before any patient-specific one. Waveform capnography should show a sustained carbon dioxide trace, confirming that the tube is in the trachea. Then oxygenation, ventilation and circulation are rechecked at once, because a deterioration now has a short list of mechanical causes as well as physiological ones: a displaced or obstructed tube, a pneumothorax, and hyperinflation from breaths given faster than the lungs can empty. Each of these can mimic the patient's original threat, and each needs a different response.

principles.title: What to check first
body: Each patient's main threat tells us what to check next. For Patient H, it is oxygenation, and whether positive pressure through the tube is recruiting lung or whether her shunt persists. For Patient P, it is pressure, and whether venous return has fallen as positive pressure was established. For Patient M, it is a blood gas soon after intubation, to compare her PaCO2 with the 15 mm Hg she was maintaining before induction. For Patient R, it is systemic pressure, right ventricular function and saturation together, because a fall in any of them can start the spiral.

In every case the first check is a measurement, not an assumption. The ventilator setting, the pressure after induction and the saturation all have to be confirmed, because the physiology has changed and the starting values no longer apply.

questions.prompt: Fifteen minutes after intubation, Patient M's repeat gas shows a PaCO2 of 24 mm Hg and her bicarbonate is still 5 mmol/L. Predict her pH and say what it means for the ventilator.
questions.answer: Her pH would be about 6.94, because 6.1 + log(5 / (0.03 × 24)) is 6.1 + log(6.94), about 6.94. Her PaCO2 is well above the 15 mm Hg she was maintaining before intubation, so the ventilator is not yet giving her the alveolar ventilation she was achieving herself, and her pH is much lower than her pre-intubation 7.15. Her alveolar ventilation needs to rise, by increasing rate or tidal volume or both, while watching for gas trapping, and the gas should be repeated.
questions.causalChain: pH depends on bicarbonate and PaCO2; her measured bicarbonate is still 5 mmol/L; a higher PaCO2 lowers pH; the reference is her own pre-intubation PaCO2.
questions.assumption: That her bicarbonate has not changed and that the sample is arterial.
questions.misconception: That a PaCO2 of 24 is low enough because it is below normal.

questions.prompt: A man with severe asthma is intubated, and his pressure falls over the next few minutes as he is ventilated at a fast rate. Using Patients P and R, explain what may be happening.
questions.answer: Fast ventilation in a patient with obstructed airways may not allow full exhalation, so gas is trapped and intrinsic PEEP builds up. Rising intrathoracic pressure raises right atrial pressure and reduces venous return, as in Patient P. Hyperinflated lung also stretches the pulmonary vessels and raises pulmonary vascular resistance, adding load to the right ventricle, as in Patient R. Together, these can cause hypotension and, if unchecked, arrest. Reducing the rate and allowing longer exhalation lowers the trapped volume and usually improves pressure.
questions.causalChain: Fast rate in obstruction leads to incomplete exhalation; gas trapping and intrinsic PEEP rise; intrathoracic pressure rises; venous return falls; PVR rises; right ventricular load rises; pressure falls.
questions.assumption: That there is no pneumothorax and that his circulating volume is not the main problem.
questions.misconception: That falling pressure after intubation is always caused by drugs.

principles.title: Back to the four patients
body: Before induction, Patient H's own fast breathing was keeping a reduced oxygen store refilled while shunt held her on the steep part of the curve. Apnea interrupted that refilling, and her high consumption drew the store down quickly. Positive pressure before apnea was the most direct way to enlarge the store and recruit what lung could be recruited, and after the tube, a saturation that fell or would not hold was the sign that the anticipated failure was occurring.

Patient P's circulation was being sustained by high sympathetic tone and the help that negative intrathoracic pressure gives venous return. Induction could reduce that tone, and positive pressure could then raise right atrial pressure against an already low upstream pressure. Restoring lost volume and avoiding excessive breaths addressed that mechanism, and a falling blood pressure in the minutes after induction would show that it was failing.

Patient M was holding her pH up with very high ventilation. Apnea stopped it, and an ordinary ventilator setting would replace it with much less. The remedy was to keep apnea short and restore her alveolar ventilation, and a PaCO2 above her pre-intubation value on an early gas would show the failure.

Patient R depended on a low pulmonary vascular resistance and enough systemic pressure to perfuse his right ventricle. Hypoxemia and hypercapnia during apnea, a lower systemic pressure after induction, and overinflation once he was ventilated could each push that ventricle into the spiral, and falling systemic pressure would be the warning. For him the first question was whether a tube was needed at all.
None of these depends on a single drug, device, or technique. Each depends on naming the threat before induction and thinking about how intubation will change it.

Worsening acidemia
Keep apnea short; restore her alveolar ventilation
Early blood gas against her pre-intubation PaCO2 of 15 mm Hg
R, massive pulmonary embolism
A right ventricle at the edge of its reserve
Right ventricular failure
Avoid hypoxemia, hypercapnia, overinflation and falls in systemic pressure
Systemic pressure, saturation and right ventricular function together

principles.title: Synthesis
body: The physiologically difficult airway is not one condition but four kinds of dependence: on a reduced oxygen store, on sympathetic tone and venous return, on compensatory ventilation, and on a right ventricle with no reserve. Intubation removes spontaneous breathing, often reduces sympathetic tone, replaces negative intrathoracic pressure, and adds apnea and positive pressure. Each patient is endangered by the part of that change that their physiology cannot absorb.

The evidence covered here, from PREOXI, PreVent, PREPARE II and FELLOW, answers specific questions in specific populations. It supports positive pressure preoxygenation and ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy for patients like those enrolled, without showing that aspiration risk is the same. It shows that a routine fluid bolus did not significantly decrease collapse in patients receiving positive-pressure ventilation during intubation. It leaves the value of apneic oxygenation in critical illness uncertain, because the one trial tested a single technique at a single center. It does not replace the physiology, which is what lets a clinician decide which part of the evidence applies to the patient in front of them.

treatmentApproach.title: Name the main threat before induction
treatmentApproach.action: Decide which form of collapse is most likely for this patient: desaturation, hypotension, worsening acidemia, or right ventricular failure. Say it aloud to the team.
treatmentApproach.why: Each patient depends on something intubation removes or is harmed by something it adds. Naming the threat sets what to prepare and what to watch first.

treatmentApproach.title: Fill the oxygen store
treatmentApproach.action: Preoxygenate with a tight seal and enough time, aiming for an end-tidal oxygen above 85 percent where it can be measured. Where shunt or a small aerated volume limits the result, consider positive pressure before apnea.
treatmentApproach.why: Desaturation during apnea depends on the available oxygen store, oxygen consumption, shunt, starting oxygenation and any oxygen entering during the apneic interval; open, denitrogenated lung holds far more oxygen. A full store does not correct shunt, so a good end-tidal reading can still accompany a low saturation.

treatmentApproach.title: Keep apnea short and supported
treatmentApproach.action: Keep the interval without ventilation short. Consider oxygen during apnea and gentle breaths between induction and laryngoscopy, weighing aspiration risk.
treatmentApproach.why: Oxygen is consumed and carbon dioxide accumulates during apnea; saturation falls steeply once PaO2 reaches the steep part of the curve.

treatmentApproach.title: Prepare for the fall in pressure
treatmentApproach.action: Assess whether the circulation is underfilled, restore lost volume where it is, and have support for pressure ready before induction. Ventilate with modest breaths after the tube.
treatmentApproach.why: Induction lowers tone and mean systemic filling pressure; positive pressure raises right atrial pressure; together they reduce venous return.

treatmentApproach.title: Match compensatory ventilation
treatmentApproach.action: If breathing is compensating for metabolic acidosis, restore the alveolar ventilation the patient was achieving once the tube is in and confirm with an early blood gas.
treatmentApproach.why: An ordinary setting removes the compensation and lets PaCO2 rise and pH fall sharply.

treatmentApproach.title: Protect the right ventricle
treatmentApproach.action: Ask first whether a tube is needed. If it is, avoid hypoxemia, hypercapnia, high intrathoracic pressure and falls in systemic pressure.
treatmentApproach.why: RV perfusion falls with systemic pressure while its load rises with pulmonary vascular resistance, which can start a self-reinforcing spiral.

treatmentApproach.title: Reassess in the first minutes
treatmentApproach.action: Confirm tube position with waveform capnography, then recheck saturation, pressure and ventilation at once. Consider tube displacement or obstruction, pneumothorax and hyperinflation, and act on each finding against the threat you named.
treatmentApproach.why: Collapse often occurs in the minutes after placement; in one series (Heffner and colleagues), the median time to cardiac arrest was about 6 minutes.
